questions.q: Write the interval notation for the set {x ∈ R : -3 ≤ x < 5}.
questions.a: [-3, 5). A wrong answer like (-3, 5) reveals the student does not distinguish between ≤ (square bracket) and < (parenthesis). Writing [-3, 5] would mean they missed that the upper bound is strict.

questions.q: Explain why the interval (2, 2) is empty, but the interval [2, 2] is not.
questions.a: (2,2) = {x ∈ R : 2 < x < 2} has no real numbers because no number is strictly greater than 2 and strictly less than 2 simultaneously. [2,2] = {x ∈ R : 2 ≤ x ≤ 2} contains exactly the single number 2. A student who says both are empty or both contain 2 confuses the strict vs. non-strict inequality conditions.

questions.q: Convert the interval (-∞, 7] into set-builder notation and state its length.
questions.a: Set-builder: {x ∈ R : x ≤ 7}. Length is not defined (infinite). A student who writes {x ∈ R : x < 7} misreads the bracket at 7. A student who gives a numerical length (e.g., 7 or ∞) does not understand that length is only defined for bounded intervals (b - a).

questions.q: Given intervals A = [1, 4) and B = (3, 6], which of the following numbers belong to A ∩ B? Choose all that apply: 1, 3, 3.5, 4, 5.
questions.a: Only 3.5. A = {x: 1 ≤ x < 4}, B = {x: 3 < x ≤ 6}. Intersection requires 1 ≤ x < 4 AND 3 < x ≤ 6 → 3 < x < 4. 1 is not >3; 3 is not >3; 4 is not <4; 5 is not <4. A student choosing 3 or 4 does not handle the mixed strict/non-strict boundaries correctly.

questions.q: A student writes the solution set of the inequality 2x - 5 ≤ 3 as x ∈ (-∞, 4). Is this correct? Justify.
questions.a: Incorrect. Solving: 2x ≤ 8 → x ≤ 4. The solution set is (-∞, 4] (including 4). The student used a parenthesis at 4, which excludes 4, but the inequality is non-strict (≤). This reveals confusion between strict and non-strict inequalities when converting to interval notation.

questions.q: Create a real-world scenario (using Indian context) that can be modeled by the interval [500, 2000) and explain what the endpoints represent.
questions.a: Example: "A metro ride in Delhi costs between ₹500 and ₹2000 per month for a daily commuter, where ₹500 is the minimum monthly pass cost (included) and ₹2000 is the maximum before a different fare slab applies (excluded)." Endpoints: 500 = minimum cost (inclusive), 2000 = upper limit of this slab (exclusive). A poor answer uses abstract numbers without context or misassigns inclusion/exclusion.
